summary: Describes an SMTP extension that lets a server and client switch to transport-layer security to get private, authenticated communication. It protects mail against eavesdroppers and attackers. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3207.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people begin a talk in the open, then agree to move into a private room. This lets mail servers do that midway through their conversation.

subtitle: Upgrade SMTP connections to encryption mid-conversation.

tldr.problem: SMTP servers and clients communicate in the clear over the Internet, exposing messages to eavesdropping and attack. Both sides need a way to authenticate each other.
tldr.mechanism: The STARTTLS extension lets a client request that the server upgrade their connection to encrypted TLS. After encryption is established, the SMTP protocol resets and normal mail delivery continues securely.
tldr.outcome: Mail servers can protect some or all of their traffic from eavesdroppers. However, STARTTLS only secures the connection between two servers, not the entire mail path from sender to recipient. RFC 3207 replaced this specification.

facts.label: State after TLS
facts.value: SMTP protocol resets to initial state

today: RFC 3207 replaced this specification in 2002 with updated SMTP TLS guidance.

sections.title: The Need for Secure SMTP
sections.content:
SMTP, the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, moves email from one server to another. Normally this happens in the clear: anyone with access to the network between servers can read or alter the mail. An untrusted router or an attacker who gains control of network traffic can spy on messages, forge mail, or inject malicious content.

Additionally, SMTP servers often want to authenticate each other, to ensure they are talking to the real server for a domain rather than an imposter. The STARTTLS extension provides a way to establish both privacy and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Email was designed when networks were small and trusted. Now that spies can listen in, mail servers need a private channel with a password check on each end.

sections.title: How STARTTLS Works
sections.content:
STARTTLS is an extension to SMTP that allows the client to request an upgrade to TLS (Transport Layer Security, the encryption protocol also known as SSL). The extension is announced by the server in response to an EHLO greeting. If the client wants to use it, the client sends the STARTTLS command.

Upon receiving a success response, the client and server perform a TLS handshake. During the handshake, they exchange certificates and negotiate encryption algorithms. Once the handshake completes, all traffic is encrypted and integrity-checked.

After successful TLS negotiation, the SMTP conversation resets to its initial state. The server discards any information it learned about the client prior to encryption (such as which SMTP extensions the client supports), and the client does the same. The client then issues an EHLO command to re-announce its identity and capabilities, and mail delivery proceeds normally but now protected by encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The server says 'I support STARTTLS'. The client asks to start it. They shake hands and set up encryption. Then they start talking again from scratch, only this time secretly.

sections.title: The STARTTLS Command
sections.content:
The STARTTLS keyword takes no parameters. The client sends a bare STARTTLS command.

The server responds with one of three codes:

  • 220 Ready to start TLS: The server is ready. The client must begin TLS negotiation immediately.
  • 501 Syntax error: The client sent parameters (which is not allowed).
  • 454 TLS not available: The server cannot start TLS due to a temporary condition (such as a missing certificate).

An important rule: a publicly referenced SMTP server (one that appears in DNS mail exchange records) MUST NOT require STARTTLS to receive mail, because that would break the Internet's mail infrastructure. However, a non-public server can choose to refuse mail until the client issues STARTTLS.

If the client uses pipelining (sending multiple SMTP commands in one batch), the STARTTLS command must be the last one in the batch.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks nicely. The server says yes or explains why not. If yes, they immediately encrypt.

sections.title: What STARTTLS Protects and Doesn't
sections.content:
STARTTLS protects the connection between two mail servers: it keeps eavesdroppers from seeing the mail headers, addresses or content as it travels between those two specific servers. It can also authenticate each server to the other if certificates are validated correctly.

However, STARTTLS is not end-to-end security. Email typically travels through multiple servers on its way from sender to recipient. Encrypting one hop does not encrypt the entire path. A message that passes through five mail servers is only protected on the hops where both servers support and use STARTTLS.

Additionally, STARTTLS between two servers does not authenticate the original sender. An SMTP server can authenticate the server that delivered a message to it, but that does not prove who wrote the message. For end-to-end authentication of the author, other mechanisms like S/MIME must be used.

Both client and server must verify the result of TLS negotiation and decide whether the security is acceptable. Simply ignoring failed checks defeats the security.

A man-in-the-middle attack is possible if a network attacker deletes the '250 STARTTLS' line from the server's EHLO response. The client will think the server does not support TLS and will proceed unencrypted. A client can defend against this by recording whether a server offers TLS and raising an alarm if that support disappears in a later session, but doing so must not cause email to bounce.
sections.plainLanguage: STARTTLS secures one part of a mail's journey, not all of it. It authenticates the server you're talking to, not who wrote the mail. It is not foolproof against an attacker who controls the network.

sections.title: Today
sections.content: RFC 3207 obsoleted this specification and provides updated guidance on SMTP security.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is outdated. A newer version exists.
